title: Sampling distributions and estimation
calculator: Four-function calculator allowed; supplied nontrivial values.
study_note: All questions, answers, and explanations are public. Numerical examples are illustrative classroom scenarios.
quiz_prompt: Quiz me from this statistics unit bank, one question at a time. Keep all four choices visible, but withhold the correct answer and explanation until I respond. Ask me to explain my reasoning. Then give feedback, cite the question ID, and revisit missed concepts later. Use a mix of skill groups. Do not invent harder calculations.

groups.name: CLT assumptions, shape, and sampling quality

questions.stem: A researcher takes 1,000 samples of 25 packages and plots each sample mean. What does one plotted value represent?
questions.explanation: A sampling distribution records a statistic from each repeated sample.
choices: The mean of all 25,000 packages combined.
A population parameter that changes on each sample.

questions.stem: In 1,000 repetitions, each sample contains 25 independent observations. What n belongs in SD/sqrt(n) for the mean?
questions.explanation: The sample size is observations per mean, not the number of repetitions.

questions.stem: A population has mean 50. Where are unbiased random-sample means centered?
questions.explanation: The expected sample mean equals the population mean under the sampling assumptions.

questions.stem: Which quantity describes how sample means vary from sample to sample?
questions.explanation: Standard error is the SD of a statistic's sampling distribution.
choices: The range of all individuals alone.

questions.stem: Individual masses have SD 20 g; means of 25 independent masses have SD 4 g. Which spread applies to one package?
questions.explanation: The individual distribution keeps its own SD; the mean uses a smaller SE.

questions.stem: Larger independent samples yield less variable means. Does this make individual packages less variable?
questions.explanation: Averaging improves precision of the statistic without changing the population.
choices: No; population spread stays the same.
Yes; every package moves toward the mean.
Only if more samples are plotted.

questions.stem: A histogram is made from 500 means, each based on 20 observations. How many values are in that histogram?
questions.explanation: Each sample contributes one statistic, so there are 500 plotted means.

questions.stem: A shipment contains 36 packages. Which variable answers the question of average mass per package in that shipment?
questions.explanation: The requested average is a statistic across the shipment's packages.

questions.stem: Sample size rises from 25 to 100 under unbiased independent sampling. What happens to the center of sample means?
questions.explanation: Sample size changes precision, not the expected sample-mean center.
choices: It stays at the population mean.

questions.stem: The population mean is unknown. Why are repeated-sample models useful for estimation?
questions.explanation: Knowing sampling variability helps express uncertainty in an estimate.
choices: They guarantee every sample equals the population.
They describe how far a sample mean might vary around that population mean.
They make the population mean change randomly every day.
They remove the need for representative sampling.

questions.stem: Population SD is 12 and n=36, with independent observations. sqrt(36)=6. What is the mean's SE?
questions.explanation: Divide population SD by the supplied square root of sample size.

questions.stem: Independent sample size quadruples with population SD fixed. What happens to SE of the mean?
questions.explanation: SE scales as 1/sqrt(n), so a fourfold n reduces it by a factor of two.

questions.stem: To halve SE, how must an independent sample's size change?
questions.explanation: Squaring the desired precision factor gives the sample-size factor.
choices: Add 4 regardless of its current size.

questions.stem: Population SD doubles while sample size stays fixed. What happens to SE?
questions.explanation: SE is proportional to population SD at fixed n.

questions.stem: Sample means are centered at 40 with SE 2. Which mean is 1.5 SE above center?
questions.explanation: Add 1.5 times 2 to the center.

questions.stem: Population mean is 20; SE of sample means is 2. An observed sample mean is 24. What standardized distance does it have?
questions.explanation: Its deviation is 4, or 2 standard errors.

questions.stem: For a normal population, compare one mass exceeding mean+2 g with the mean of 100 independent masses exceeding the same cutoff. Which is more likely?
questions.explanation: Averaging narrows the distribution around the same center.

figure.alt: Two normal densities centered at the same mean: one observation is wider, and a mean of 100 is narrower. A common cutoff above the mean is marked.

data.alt: Two normal densities centered at the same mean: one observation is wider, and a mean of 100 is narrower. A common cutoff above the mean is marked.

questions.stem: Two samples have the same observed mean above a claimed population mean and the same population SD, but sizes 25 and 100. Which mean is farther above in SE units?
questions.explanation: The larger sample has smaller SE, making the same absolute gap more SE units.
choices: The larger sample changes the claimed mean.

questions.stem: SE is 4 at n=25. What is SE at n=100, with the same population SD and independence?
questions.explanation: Quadrupling n halves SE.

questions.stem: Increasing n from 100 to 400 halves SE. Would adding the same 300 observations to any starting n always halve SE?
questions.explanation: The square-root relation depends on the multiplicative change in n.
choices: No; the ratio of sample sizes matters.
Yes; SE depends only on added observations.
Yes; an extra 300 always halves it.

questions.skill_group: CLT assumptions, shape, and sampling quality
questions.stem: The CLT supports an approximately normal distribution of large-sample means. What does it not claim?
questions.explanation: The CLT concerns the average or sum, not a transformation of population shape.
choices: Larger independent samples can have smaller SE.
Means can have approximately normal sampling distributions.

questions.skill_group: CLT assumptions, shape, and sampling quality
questions.stem: Independent observations come from an exactly normal population. Is n>=30 necessary for their mean to be normal?
questions.explanation: Independent normal observations have an exactly normal average.
choices: Yes; normal means are impossible below 30.
Yes; individual normality disappears in small samples.
No; the mean instead becomes uniform.
No; their mean is normal for any positive sample size.

questions.skill_group: CLT assumptions, shape, and sampling quality
questions.stem: A population is strongly right-skewed and n=5. What is the best judgment about a normal model for the mean?
questions.explanation: Small samples may retain substantial population skewness.
choices: It is exact for every skewed population.
It is guaranteed by the existence of a mean.

questions.skill_group: CLT assumptions, shape, and sampling quality
questions.stem: Someone says n=30 guarantees normal sample means for every population. What is the problem?
questions.explanation: There is no universal cutoff guaranteeing a good normal approximation.
choices: Thirty is too large for any sample.
Sample means can never approach normality.
Skewness and extreme observations affect how large n needs to be.
Only populations with mean zero qualify.

questions.skill_group: CLT assumptions, shape, and sampling quality
questions.stem: Fifty readings taken seconds apart from one fluctuating machine are treated as independent. What should be checked?
questions.explanation: Correlation can undermine the usual independent-observation SE formula.
choices: Whether the mean can be calculated.

questions.skill_group: CLT assumptions, shape, and sampling quality
questions.stem: A sample of 200 is drawn without replacement from 500. Does it meet the course's at-most-10% independence guideline?
questions.explanation: The sample fraction is 200/500, well above 10%.
choices: Yes; every random sample meets the guideline.
No; samples must contain fewer than 10 observations.
No; it is 40% of the population.

questions.skill_group: CLT assumptions, shape, and sampling quality
questions.stem: Only successful downloads are sampled to estimate duration for all attempts. Does a small SE remove that selection problem?
questions.explanation: A precise estimate can still target the wrong population because of biased coverage.
choices: Yes; enough successful downloads represent failures automatically.
Yes; a normal curve proves unbiased selection.
No; SE must equal the mean.
No; precision does not correct selection bias.

questions.skill_group: CLT assumptions, shape, and sampling quality
questions.stem: A sample grows from 50 to 51 observations. Must its mean move closer to the population mean?
questions.explanation: Long-run stabilization does not guarantee improvement at each additional observation.
choices: Yes; the law of large numbers guarantees monotone improvement.
No; individual additions can move it either way.
Yes; every increase improves the estimate.
No; larger samples always worsen estimates.

questions.skill_group: CLT assumptions, shape, and sampling quality
questions.stem: For independent observations with finite variance, compare repeated means at n=1 and n=100. What is generally expected?
questions.explanation: Averaging reduces spread, and CLT behavior can change the sampling-distribution shape.
choices: The n=1 histogram must be normal.
Means at n=100 are less spread and often more nearly normal.
The population itself becomes less spread.

questions.skill_group: CLT assumptions, shape, and sampling quality
questions.stem: All individual waits lie between 2 and 14. A normal approximation gives a tiny chance that a mean is below 2. How should this be interpreted?
questions.explanation: An average cannot fall below the minimum possible individual value.
choices: The true sample mean can actually be below every observation.
The normal model is exact at every tail.
It is approximation error outside the true support.
The observations must include negative waits.

questions.stem: Twenty items have sample mean mass 5 g. What is their total mass?
questions.explanation: Sample sum equals n times sample mean.

questions.stem: Individual mean mass is 3 g. What is the expected total for 10 items?
questions.explanation: Expected totals add, though actual totals vary.

questions.stem: For independent items, the SD of a sum is sqrt(n) times individual SD. Why is n times SD generally wrong?
questions.explanation: Adding variances gives n times variance, hence sqrt(n) times SD.
choices: All individual deviations have the same sign.
Independent variances add; SD is then a square root.

questions.stem: The number of independent items rises from 25 to 100. What happens to expected sum and SD of sum?
questions.explanation: Sum mean scales with n and sum SD with sqrt(n).
choices: Expected sum stays fixed; SD halves.

questions.stem: Independent sample size increases. What happens to spread in original units?
questions.explanation: Totals aggregate variation while averages divide the total by n.
choices: SD of sums rises; SE of averages falls.

questions.stem: For n=20, a total exceeding 240 is equivalent to which mean event?
questions.explanation: Divide the total cutoff by the fixed sample size.

questions.stem: A sum event and its equivalent mean event use correctly matched centers and SDs. How do their z-scores compare?
questions.explanation: Scaling numerator and denominator by n leaves standardization unchanged.
choices: The mean z-score is always zero.
The sum z-score is n times larger.

questions.stem: A fixed 5-kg container is added to a shipment of random item masses. What changes?
questions.explanation: A fixed additive quantity shifts the distribution without adding random variability.
choices: Both mean and SD rise by 5 kg.
Expected total rises by 5 kg; total SD is unchanged.

questions.stem: All items in a batch tend to be heavy or light together. What is questionable about sqrt(n) times individual SD for the total?
questions.explanation: Positive dependence can make total variation larger than the independent formula predicts.

questions.stem: A sum distribution has mean 100 and SD 4. What total is 2 SD above its mean?
questions.explanation: Add two times the sum's SD to its mean.

source.slide_title: A specified distance for a sum

questions.stem: A question asks whether the combined duration of 40 tasks exceeds one hour. Which variable should be modeled?
questions.explanation: The requested event is about total duration.

questions.stem: An exponential population has mean 5. Which is generally more unusual under independent sampling: one duration above 7 or 100 durations averaging above 7?
questions.explanation: The average is far less variable around the same mean.

questions.stem: A supplied sampling model gives P(mean<=12)=0.90. What is P(mean>12)?
questions.explanation: The two events are complements.

questions.stem: A supplied normal distribution of sample means gives cumulative probabilities 0.15 at 8 and 0.85 at 12. What is the probability between 8 and 12?
questions.explanation: Subtract cumulative areas at the endpoints.

questions.stem: The 95th percentile of a sample-mean distribution is 14. What does it describe?
questions.explanation: The percentile belongs to the sampling distribution, not automatically the individual distribution.
choices: 95% of all individuals must be at most 14.
About 95% of repeated sample means are at most 14.

questions.stem: The course's binomial normal approximation check requires np>5 and n(1-p)>5. For n=100, p=0.02, which judgment fits?
questions.explanation: Both expected-count requirements must hold.
choices: It passes because p is positive.
It fails because expected failures are 98.
It fails because expected successes are only 2.

questions.stem: Why approximate P(X=40) for a binomial count using a normal interval around 40 instead of a single point?
questions.explanation: Continuity correction represents an integer count by a one-unit interval.
choices: A continuous model assigns zero probability to one exact point.
A normal model has no area.

questions.stem: Which continuous event uses the appropriate continuity correction for X>=45?
questions.explanation: The included count 45 contributes the interval beginning at 44.5.

questions.stem: Which continuous event approximates X<=45 with continuity correction?
questions.explanation: Including the entire count-45 interval extends the upper boundary to 45.5.

questions.stem: Which interval approximates the discrete event X=45?
questions.explanation: The one-unit interval around 45 represents its discrete probability mass.

questions.stem: Why report a confidence interval instead of only a sample mean?
questions.explanation: An interval communicates estimation precision beyond a single point estimate.
choices: It expresses uncertainty in estimating the population mean.
It guarantees the true mean is the midpoint.

questions.stem: Sample mean is 12 and margin of error is 2. What interval results?
questions.explanation: Add and subtract the margin from the estimate.

figure.alt: Interval from 10 to 14 with its center marked at 12.

data.alt: Interval from 10 to 14 with its center marked at 12.

questions.stem: A symmetric confidence interval is 8 to 12. What point estimate is at its center?
questions.explanation: The midpoint is the estimate, not either endpoint.

questions.stem: A symmetric interval is 8 to 12. What is the margin of error?
questions.explanation: Margin of error is half the total width.

questions.stem: What does a 95% confidence procedure mean in repeated appropriate sampling?
questions.explanation: Confidence describes long-run coverage by the method.
choices: Every interval has 95% of its length below the mean.
95% of observations lie in every interval.
About 95% of intervals constructed this way contain the fixed population mean in the long run.
The sample mean equals the population mean 95% of the time.

questions.stem: One hundred valid 95% intervals are constructed in repeated sampling. Must exactly 95 cover the mean?
questions.explanation: A long-run proportion is not an exact finite-sample quota.
choices: No; the coverage count itself can vary.
Yes; any other count proves bias.
Yes; the confidence level fixes that count.

questions.stem: After a specific interval is computed, what is correct about its relation to a fixed population mean?
questions.explanation: Frequentist coverage refers to random intervals before observing the data.
choices: The endpoints must equal the smallest and largest observation.
The fixed mean changes to fit it with probability 95%.
The mean occupies 95% of the interval.
It either contains that mean or does not; 95% describes the procedure.

questions.stem: A 95% mean interval is 10 to 14 minutes. Does this say 95% of individual durations lie there?
questions.explanation: An interval for a parameter is different from an interval covering individual values.
choices: Yes; the mean and individuals have identical spread.
No; it estimates the population mean.
No; it instead guarantees every duration lies there.
Yes; that is the meaning of any confidence interval.

questions.stem: A mean interval is 10 to 14. How should a proposed mean of 12 be described?
questions.explanation: Every interior value is compatible with the interval; the midpoint is not a certainty.
choices: Compatible with the interval, without being proved exact.
Proved to be the exact population mean.

figure.alt: Interval 10 to 14 and proposed mean 12 marked at the center.

data.alt: Interval 10 to 14 and proposed mean 12 marked at the center.

questions.stem: A mean interval is 10 to 14 minutes. Which report matches its target?
questions.explanation: The reported target is the population mean, with confidence understood as procedure coverage.
choices: Exactly 95 of the next 100 durations will lie there.
The procedure estimates the population mean duration between 10 and 14 minutes.
The median is guaranteed to equal 12.
Every future duration will be between 10 and 14.

questions.stem: Using the same sample and method, confidence rises from 90% to 99%. What happens to interval width?
questions.explanation: Higher coverage requires a larger critical multiplier and a wider interval.

questions.stem: For known population SD and fixed confidence, n quadruples. What happens to the margin of error?
questions.explanation: The mean interval margin scales with 1/sqrt(n).

questions.stem: At fixed n and confidence, known population SD doubles. What happens to interval width?
questions.explanation: Margin and full width are proportional to population SD.

questions.stem: A known-SD mean interval currently has margin 1. To target margin 0.5 at the same confidence, how should n change?
questions.explanation: Halving a square-root-based margin requires four times the observations.

questions.stem: A sample-size formula returns 62.2 observations. Which planned integer size meets that minimum?
questions.explanation: Round a required minimum up to avoid falling short.

questions.stem: A narrow interval uses only the fastest successful jobs to estimate the mean for all jobs. What is its main limitation?
questions.explanation: Precision cannot repair systematically excluded outcomes.
choices: Biased selection can make the interval misleading despite narrow width.
Adding decimal places removes selection bias.

questions.stem: Population SD is known and the sample is large. What still needs checking for the usual mean interval?
questions.explanation: A known SD does not replace sampling and dependence assumptions.
choices: Whether every observation equals the mean.
Whether the mean is a whole number.

questions.stem: A symmetric 90% confidence construction leaves what fraction in each tail?
questions.explanation: The excluded 10% splits equally across two tails.

questions.stem: For a known-SD mean interval, supplied SE=0.5 and critical multiplier=2. What is the margin of error?
questions.explanation: Margin equals critical multiplier times SE.

questions.stem: From the same sample, a 90% and 99% mean interval are built with the same method. Which statement fits?
questions.explanation: Changing confidence changes the critical multiplier, not the observed estimate.
choices: The 99% interval has a different sample mean.
The 99% interval is wider but has the same center.

questions.stem: A sample contains 100 observations, but population SD is unknown. Does large n make that SD known?
questions.explanation: A larger sample can improve an estimate but does not make the parameter known.
choices: Yes; n>=30 makes population SD exact.
No; the sample mean must also be unknown.
Yes; the sample SD becomes the population parameter by definition.
No; it is still estimated from data.

questions.stem: To estimate a population mean with unknown population SD using a sample SD, which standard method fits?
questions.explanation: The t method accounts for estimating population SD.
choices: A proportion interval regardless of variable type.
A known-SD z interval treating s as known population SD.

questions.stem: Why does a t interval use a larger critical multiplier than z at small degrees of freedom?
questions.explanation: The t reference distribution reflects additional variability from estimating SD.
choices: The population mean is random in the formula.
Estimating SD adds uncertainty reflected in heavier tails.
The observations must all be larger.

questions.stem: A one-sample t interval uses n=16. What degrees of freedom are used?
questions.explanation: A one-sample mean t method uses n-1 degrees of freedom.

questions.stem: Which t distribution has heavier tails?
questions.explanation: Small degrees of freedom produce heavier tails and greater critical values.

questions.stem: A small random independent sample comes from a normal population. Is n<30 alone a reason to reject a t interval?
questions.explanation: Conditions matter; small n is not an automatic disqualification for normal data.
choices: Yes; t requires at least 30 in every case.
No; it must use a proportion interval.
No; small normal samples can support the t method.

questions.stem: A sample of 6 has strong skewness and an extreme outlier. What is sensible about a t interval?
questions.explanation: The small sample may not support the normality assumptions of the usual t method.
choices: It is automatically reliable because t has heavy tails.
The outlier must be removed without investigation.
Six observations guarantee a normal sampling distribution.

questions.stem: Sample SD is 6 minutes and n=9; sqrt(9)=3. What estimated SE is used?
questions.explanation: Estimated SE is s/sqrt(n) and retains the measurement units.

questions.stem: For comparison, sample SD and confidence are held fixed while n increases. What happens to a t mean interval's margin?
questions.explanation: Larger n reduces estimated SE and increases degrees of freedom.
choices: It increases because there are more observations.
It decreases as SE and the critical t value decrease.

questions.stem: A report gives sample SD=6 minutes and SE=1 minute. Which describes variation among individual observed times?
questions.explanation: Sample SD describes observed individual spread; SE describes mean-estimation precision.

questions.stem: 40 of 100 sampled jobs succeed. What is the sample success proportion?
questions.explanation: Divide the success count by the sample size.

questions.stem: Which question targets a population proportion?
questions.explanation: A proportion summarizes membership in a defined yes/no outcome.
choices: What is the mean duration of jobs?
What is the SD of file sizes?
What is the median number of pages?
What fraction of jobs finish on time?

questions.stem: The success proportion is 0.35. What is the failure proportion?
questions.explanation: Binary outcome proportions add to 1.

questions.stem: A report gives 30 successes among 120 observations. Which is the estimate of population success proportion?
questions.explanation: The success count must be divided by the total to estimate the proportion.

questions.stem: A proportion estimate is 0.40 with margin 0.05. What interval is this in percentages?
questions.explanation: Convert the endpoints 0.35 and 0.45 to percentages.

questions.stem: A 95% confidence interval estimates a population use rate. Does 95% mean that 95% of the population uses the service?
questions.explanation: Confidence level and the estimated parameter are different quantities.
choices: No; 95% describes the interval procedure's coverage.
No; it means 95 people were surveyed.
Yes; confidence equals the use rate.

questions.stem: A population proportion interval is 0.30 to 0.42. How should a proposed proportion 0.50 be described?
questions.explanation: Being outside this interval is evidence against compatibility, not an absolute impossibility statement.
choices: Proved impossible under every future sample.
Compatible because 0.50 is a valid probability.
Outside the interval and incompatible with this interval estimate.

figure.alt: A proportion interval 0.30 to 0.42 with proposed value 0.50 to its right.

data.alt: A proportion interval 0.30 to 0.42 with proposed value 0.50 to its right.

questions.stem: A symmetric proportion interval is 0.20 to 0.30. What is the estimate and margin?
questions.explanation: The midpoint is 0.25 and half-width is 0.05.

questions.stem: A proportion interval is 20% to 30%. Which conclusion matches the target?
questions.explanation: The target is a population yes/no percentage, not a numerical measurement mean.
choices: The population percentage is estimated between 20% and 30%.
Every individual has a value between 20 and 30.
Exactly 25% of the sample must be successful.
The mean duration is between 20 and 30 minutes.

questions.stem: A rate estimate rises from 40% to 45%. What is its increase in percentage points?
questions.explanation: Percentage-point difference subtracts the percentages directly, unlike relative percent increase.

questions.stem: The course's ordinary normal-approximation interval check requires more than 5 observed successes and more than 5 failures. Which sample passes?
questions.explanation: Both observed counts must exceed 5 under the stated convention.

questions.stem: A sample has 2 successes and 98 failures. Does a large total alone justify the ordinary normal-approximation proportion interval?
questions.explanation: The success-failure check concerns both counts, not just total n.
choices: No; proportions cannot be estimated at all.
No; the observed success count is too sparse.

questions.stem: Everyone in a few selected clubs is surveyed. What challenges treating all responses as independent?
questions.explanation: Cluster membership can introduce within-group dependence.
choices: The sample proportion cannot be computed.
Members of the same club may have correlated responses.
Randomly selecting clubs guarantees individual independence.
Club members cannot have binary responses.

questions.stem: 400 people are sampled without replacement from 20,000. Does this meet the at-most-10% sample-fraction guideline?
questions.explanation: 400/20,000=0.02, within the stated guideline.
choices: Yes; any random sample meets it.

questions.stem: Using the same sample and interval method, confidence increases. What happens to the proportion margin?
questions.explanation: The higher-confidence critical multiplier increases the margin.
choices: The sample proportion becomes the confidence level.

questions.stem: For a comparison holding the observed proportion and confidence fixed, n quadruples. What happens to estimated margin?
questions.explanation: The estimated SE and margin scale with 1/sqrt(n).

questions.stem: Why use planning proportion 0.5 when no prior estimate is available?
questions.explanation: The largest Bernoulli variance is at p=0.5, so planning protects against smaller assumed variation.
choices: It guarantees half the population has the trait.
It maximizes p(1-p), giving a conservative required sample size.
It minimizes all margins to zero.
It makes the sample unbiased automatically.

questions.stem: An open voluntary poll has 50,000 replies and a very small calculated margin. What remains uncertain?
questions.explanation: A conventional sampling margin does not account for voluntary-response selection bias.
choices: Whether its respondents represent the target population.
Whether the calculated margin must be negative.

questions.stem: The plus-four estimate adds two successes and two failures. With 8 successes out of 40, what adjusted fraction is used?
questions.explanation: The adjusted count is x+2 and the adjusted total is n+4.

questions.stem: The slides recommend plus-four when confidence is at least 90% and n>=10. Does n=24 at 85% confidence meet that recommendation?
questions.explanation: Both stated recommendations must be met; this is distinct from the ordinary interval count check.
choices: Yes; plus-four has no stated conditions.
No; the confidence level is below the stated threshold.
